newsitem.title: BELGIUM: British widow faces Belgian insemination hurdles.
newsitem.headline: British widow faces Belgian insemination hurdles.

text.p: A British widow who won a long legal battle to take her late husband's sperm to Belgium for artificial insemination faces tough vetting when she gets here, specialists said on Friday.

On Thursday Britain's Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority reversed an earlier ruling and decided to allow Diane Blood, 32, to export her husband Stephen's sperm, frozen since he died suddenly in 1995 without leaving permission for his semen to be used.

"Post-mortem insemination is very debatable. These are special demands and therefore need some special attention," Professor Paul Devroey of Brussels' Academisch Ziekenhuis, Belgium's leading fertility clinic, told Reuters on Friday.
The clinic, part of Brussels Free University, conducts some 2,000 artificial inseminations a year but hardly ever gets requests for insemination using the sperm of a dead partner.

"When we receive such demands there normally has to be written consent from both partners to use the sperm. Then there is a psychological analysis to establish the social environment in which the child will be born," he said.
There is also extensive counselling of the patient to assess her mental state and her motives and to explain clearly the implications of her intended course of action.

"It is a very symbolic event and one has to be very careful that the child will have the right environment...that it will not be an attempt to recreate the father which would put heavy expectations on the child," Devroey said.
He said he could only remember receiving three or four requests for post-mortem insemination, and in each case the woman had decided after counselling not to go ahead.
"There are many arguments against post-mortem artificial insemination," he said.

Devroey said that after the analysis, counselling and medical examination the team assessing such a request would meet to decide whether to agree to it. If there was any doubt they could reject it or take it to the hospital's ethics committee.
But even if the decision was positive and the woman decided to go ahead it was still far from certain that the insemination would be a success and the pregnancy would go to term.
The chances of fertilisation taking place after natural insemination are only 12 percent, Devroey said.
"With modern techniques, micro insertion and hormone stimulation treatment, it goes up a lot but it is still a long way from being guaranteed," he said.
It all depends on the health of the sperm and the age of the woman, he said.

"If the sperm is good quality, active, insemination can take place in the body. If it is not then we give the woman hormone treatment and extract the eggs and inseminate them outside the body and replace them," Devroey said.
Using all available techniques the chances of successful fertilisation are still only 50 percent in a woman of 25. This falls to just five percent at age 40.
On top of all the trauma and uncertainty is the cost.
"A straightforward insemination costs 20,000 francs ($570). An insemination using all the techniques would cost $5,000," Devroey said.
